newsitem.title: USA: US beef prices seen rebounding on stronger demand.
newsitem.headline: US beef prices seen rebounding on stronger demand.

text.p: U.S. beef prices were poised to rebound following a week and a half of steep declines that saw prices on some grades tumble $6.00 per cwt, industry sources said.

Brisk retail buying this week at the lower prices reportedly cleaned out packer supplies, which could lead to higher prices next week as retailers book for post-Easter advertising features, sources said.
"I would expect by this time next week, we should see some recovery in prices," said Chuck Levitt, livestock market analyst with Alaron Trading Corp in Chicago.
Levitt said beef prices had fallen to a level that were inviting expanded purchases by the retail meat trade, a view shared by some wholesale meat suppliers.
"This week has been pretty good for retail buying," said Keith Bollman, meat commodities analyst with Topco Associates, a supplier of meat to grocery stores across the U.S.
"I think the packers are pretty clean after this week," Bollman said. "They've had significant boxed loads moving out."

Sales of fabricated beef loads totaled 1,620 this week through midday Friday, well above 1,147 loads sold last week and 986 loads the week ended February 28, U.S. Department of Agriculture statistics showed.

Midday beef prices on Friday were quoted down $0.05 to $0.39 per hundredweight (cwt) on 302 loads sold, USDA said. Heavier-weight choice beef was quoted down $0.05 at $101.74 per cwt, reflecting a drop of $6.05 since March 4 when prices started their recent decline, USDA reported.
Bollman added that retailers were buying all cuts of beef instead of focusing on specific cuts, which indicated stronger overall demand.

When the weather warms in spring, retailers tend to focus on cuts that are popular for grilling such as steaks, Bollman said. He added that retailers had bought beef for delivery through at least the second week of April already.

The recent drop in beef prices squeezed packer operating margins, resulting in plants buying cattle "hand-to-mouth" with little interest in stockpiling beef, said Jim Robb, analyst with Livestock Marketing Information Center in Denver.
"Everybody's buying hand-to-mouth, which means that this thing can turn around very quickly at some point," Robb said.
The tight margins spurred some large packers to announce earlier this week that they were cutting back on production.
Resulting tighter beef supplies also could bolster beef prices next week, particularly if packers follow through on cutbacks next week and beyond, Bollman said.

Excel Corp, a unit of Cargill Inc Friday said it still planned to follow through on plans to reduce beef production at its six plants starting Saturday, due to unprofitable market conditions. The cutbacks will last for an indefinite period, a company official said.

IBP Inc said Wednesday it had slowed production this week at its 11 U.S. fed cattle beef plants and four cow beef boning plants. A company spokesman said IBP had trimmed operations at most plants to 40 hours or less from 48.
Officials with IBP as well as with ConAgra Inc's Monfort Red Meat Co could not be reached for comment on Friday regarding plans for next week's operations.
